title: Mali: gardens, water and regional names
description: Mali histories in Odisha through irrigation, flower markets, women’s work, a Jeypore migration tradition and regional temple services.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: Flowers connect gardens with markets and shrines. Following that journey brings different Mali histories into view: the water needed to grow a crop, the work of preparing it for sale, and the regional services that an occupational label alone cannot explain.

paragraphs.text: Thurston’s 1909 Mali entry quotes an 1871 census account of settlements where streams irrigated vegetable plots and produce was carried to markets. The original census volume has not been separately examined here.

A note about Pondra Malis adds a more particular detail. A garden owner using a picottah—a bucket lifted by a weighted lever—was reportedly expected to entertain visiting community members. The compiler presents this as information received. It is a glimpse of hospitality attached to a working garden, rather than an observed rule for every Mali household.

In a report published in 2023, Deepanwita Gita Niyogi describes flower cultivation in Mali-dominated Maliguda in Koraput. Seasonal stream water supports the gardens but declines by February. Marigolds are prominent among the flowers grown.

Women keep flowers indoors overnight and sell them the following morning in donas, or leaf bowls. The report describes November–February flower sales as supplementary work alongside vegetables and coriander. Growing, storing and selling belong to the same account of a livelihood. The visit date is unspecified, so this is a published snapshot, not a survey of present conditions.
The accounts invite comparison of water and markets; they do not establish continuous family histories or practices.

Thurston also includes C. Hayavadana Rao’s report that Malis said their ancestors came from Kasi, or Benares, to serve the Raja of Jeypore. This is a reported migration tradition. It supplies neither a verified date nor a founding charter for the community.

The Bhadrak District Gazetteer connects Mali flower and garland sales with commercial cultivation encouraged by growing demand. The short passage points to a market relationship beyond the garden, although it does not give production figures or establish the circumstances of every household.

The Ganjam District Gazetteer uses a combined Mali/Raula heading. It describes Mali flower business alongside Raula conch blowing at auspicious occasions and remuneration from offerings at Siva and Durga shrines. Those details document regional services. The combined heading does not establish that Mali and Raula are interchangeable identities throughout Odisha, or that these temple roles describe Koraput’s cultivators.

These sources explain some work and traditions associated with Mali communities. They do not show that a caste was deliberately created at one moment for gardening. A fuller history needs local accounts of families, land, migration and changing work. Neither a surname nor the occupation of growing flowers identifies someone’s caste.
